claims.statement: Colour-naming systems across languages achieve near-optimal compression in the information-bottleneck sense: mean efficiency loss eps = 0.18 (+-0.07) bits at a fitted trade-off beta_l = 1.03 (+-0.01), on the steep part of the IB curve.
claims.scope: World Color Survey (110 languages; those with >= 5 responses per chip), English; 330 chips; meanings = isotropic Gaussians in CIELAB (sigma^2 = 64); 'least informative' (LI) source prior estimated from the naming data (5-fold cross-validated over languages); beta_l chosen per language to minimise its distance to the curve.

quantities.name: ib_efficiency_loss_eps_mean
quantities.source: reanalysis/c1.py, released model (LI source, not cross-validated); paper Table 1 LI/IB 0.18 +- 0.07

quantities.name: ib_efficiency_loss_eps_median
quantities.baseline: random CONVEX partitions: Voronoi cells in CIELAB around K random chips, K = the language's number of modal terms, 40 draws per language (prior-weighted centres: 0.284, c4.py)

quantities.name: share_of_gap_to_ib_bound_closed_by_convexity
quantities.baseline: real languages close a further 0.05 beyond the median random convex partition

quantities.name: share_random_convex_partitions_as_efficient_as_language
quantities.unit: mean share of Voronoi draws with eps <= the language's mode map
quantities.baseline: the real mode map beats the median Voronoi draw in 84/102 languages (87/102 with prior-weighted centres)

our_assessment.why: Reproduces from the released model (eps 0.184 vs 0.18; beta 1.035 vs 1.03). 'Near-optimal' needs its scale, which the paper does not give: a random assignment of chips to the same number of terms sits at about 1.9 bits; a random CONVEX partition of perceptual space (Voronoi cells, no language involved) already sits at 0.29; real systems at 0.19. Convexity alone closes about 85% of the distance to the bound; actual languages close about 5 points more. That residual is real -- real systems beat the median convex partition in 84-87 of 102 languages -- but it is the language-specific part of the result, and it is small. The paper's own control (39 hue rotations of each language) cannot show this, because rotations are convex too: it tests alignment with the irregular stimulus distribution and the source prior, not efficiency against systems 'that evolved independently of F_beta'. Untested here and worth testing: the LI prior is estimated from the same naming data, which can only favour the real systems over rotations and random partitions; the uniform-source analysis (paper: eps 0.24) needs an IB curve the release does not include.

claims.statement: To rule out that IB is too permissive, each language was compared with 39 hue-rotated variants of itself: 93% of languages achieve better trade-offs than any of their variants and the rest better than most.
claims.scope: Rotation across the 40 chromatic columns of the WCS palette; achromatic column fixed.

quantities.name: share_languages_beating_all_hue_rotations
quantities.baseline: soft encoder vs all 39 rotations; median rotated eps 0.296 vs real 0.166

our_assessment.why: Reproduces (96/102 = 94%). Narrower in what it tests: a rotation keeps the system's convexity, number of terms and internal geometry and moves only its alignment with hue, so 'beats its rotations' shows that real categories sit where the perceptual space and the prior favour them -- not that languages are near-optimal compared with arbitrary alternatives. Random convex partitions score the same as rotations (0.294 vs 0.296), which is consistent with that reading.

relations.why: Both read closeness to an information-theoretic optimum as evidence of a communicative pressure without giving the distance a null-model scale. Here a random convex partition is already most of the way to the bound; there, a quantity built as a product of two negatively related factors is compressed partly by construction. In both, the residual beyond the null is real and much smaller than the headline suggests.
